Cheat-resistant grading

Source: vignettes/cheat-resistant-grading.Rmd
cheat-resistant-grading.Rmd

Versión en español

A student file is R code, and R code can change how other R code behaves. This article shows what corrector does about that, which engine to pick, and how to write tests that are hard to fool.

What each engine stops

With the callr and inproc engines the tests run in the same R process as the student code. corrector blocks the common tricks there:

  • A student object that redefines a base function the tests use (all(), ==, isTRUE(), testthat’s expect_equal(), and so on) is not visible to the tests.
  • Student S3 methods for the comparison generics (Ops, ==, all.equal, as.logical, …) are not visible to the tests either.
  • Functions written into the global environment are not visible to the tests.
  • quit() raises an error.

Allow a name with allow_masking when the exercise asks for it, for example allow_masking = "Ops.dinero" for an exercise about an S3 class.

A student who knows R well can still get around this, because their code can change the process itself: attach() a fake isTRUE(), register an S3 method with registerS3method(), or replace a base function with unlockBinding(). On these engines such code is reported (see below), but it can still change the grade.

engine = "isolated" closes that gap. The tests run in one R process and the student code in another. Each student function the tests call runs in the student process, and only its result comes back, as plain data. Nothing the student does to their own process reaches the process that compares the values. A student function that returns a function, an environment or an R expression gets an error, because those could carry code back.

results <- grade_submissions("submissions/", test_dir = "tests/",
                             engine = "isolated", workers = 4)

The cost is time: each exercise starts two R processes. On one machine, 10 students with 5 tests each took 9 s with callr and 20 s with isolated, both with one worker. workers runs students in parallel on either engine.

engine = "container" runs those two processes inside a Docker container with no network, limited memory and processes, a read-only system, and only the exercise’s files. Student code then cannot reach your files, your network or the other students’ submissions either. Build the image once from the file the package ships (add any package the students or the tests use, because the container has no network):

docker build -t corrector-runner "$(Rscript -e 'cat(system.file("container", package = "corrector"))')"

Each exercise takes a few seconds longer, because the container has to start.

Reading the notes

On every engine, corrector reads each student file before running it and reports calls such as attach(), unlockBinding(), registerS3method(), trace() or parse(text = ), and writes into the global or base environment, as suspicious code: ... in the message column. After the code runs, it reports what actually changed (attached environments, registered S3 methods, replaced base functions) as tampering: .... scan_code() runs the first check on its own.

The notes do not change a test’s status. grade_report() lists the students who got one under “Check by hand”, so you can read those files yourself:

grade_report(results)
#> ...
#> Check by hand (suspicious code or tampering, see the message column):
#>   Lopez

Tests that are hard to fool

These habits help on every engine. They stop the S3 method tricks even on callr and inproc. They do not stop attach() or replaced base functions there (a student can attach a fake identical() too); only the isolated engine stops those.

Compare with identical(). It does not dispatch on the class of its arguments, and it compares the class too, so a student object with its own == or all.equal() method does not pass:

test_ejercicio1_raices <- function() {
  identical(ceros_cuadratica(1, 0, -1), c(-1, 1))
}

For numbers that need a tolerance, check that the result is a plain number before you compare it:

test_ejercicio1_media <- function() {
  x <- media(c(1, 2, 4))
  is.double(x) && !is.object(x) && isTRUE(all.equal(x, 7 / 3))
}

With testthat, prefer expect_identical() and expect_type().

Use inputs the student cannot know in advance. A student who has seen the tests can hard-code the answers; random inputs checked against a reference solution in the test file stop that:

test_ejercicio2_ordenar <- function() {
  x <- sample(100, 20)
  identical(ordenar(x), sort(x))
}

What is still possible

  • Student code runs as your user, so it can read any file you can, including the test files and the reference solutions in them. It can also write any file you can, including corrector’s own temporary files and other students’ submissions, and start programs that outlive the grading. The isolated engine keeps student code out of the process that compares values, but it cannot stop attacks through the file system. The "container" engine does: inside the container the student only sees the files of their exercise. Still treat test files as visible to students, because the test is among those files.
  • Inside the container, student code shares the folder where the test process leaves its result. A student who studies how corrector works could, in principle, forge their own result. The container protects your computer; it does not make cheating impossible for someone who studies the package.
  • A student function returns whatever its author wants. If the tests use fixed inputs, an answer table works; random inputs stop that.
  • The checks above look for known tricks. Obfuscated code that hides them usually shows up as suspicious code (for example a call to parse(text = ) or a suspicious name inside a string), but not always.

corrector is not a sandbox. The security notes in the README say more.
